Onsite purification will likely be required because of the ultrapure need for data center cooling. 3.3 Access to Fiber or Connectivity Fiber infrastructure is becoming widespread in developed areas such as urban and suburban locations. Rural siting of a data center may lack easy access to fiber optic infrastructure. This would require planning and right-of-way to bring fiber to the site. Good connectivity to the internet and other data centers ensures that data can be transferred quickly and predictably. Redundancy through multiple service providers or through a content delivery network (CDN) can help prevent interruptions to operations. Therefore, proximity to an internet exchange point where multiple large networks integrate with one another should be considered. Sites that do not possess adequate telecommunication infrastructure including the presence of multiple carriers should be eliminated from the selection process. [1, 7, 8, 11]. Data maps of fiber lines should be used to show the proximity of such lines. This will provide an indication of the distance and diversity of fiber lines available. Bohler estimates a minimum of 40 acres for a small data center. Hyperscale data center developers will require larger tracts of land. For example, a very large data center, or hyperscale data center, will require hundreds of acres with considerable energy resources [9]. Some developers are proposing hyperscale data center parks on several thousand acres [28]. Middle-sized data centers require a footprint as small as 40 acres [2] while a hyperscale data center may require up to 200 acres [9]. Therefore, 200 acres seems to be a reasonable bounding value for the data center alone. However, additional land will be required to accommodate a collocated advanced NPP. Fifty acres or less will typically accommodate the advanced NPP. However, a data base site may want to seek more than 250 acres combined to allow for additional separation. Of course, if security is to be combined for the facilities, then a smaller footprint is more efficient. The NRC has additional siting requirements regarding NPP proximity to population centers that collocated facilities will need to consider. These are incorporated in the OR-SAGE site requirements for advanced NPPs. 3.4.1 Community Pushback Public concern about any construction project is inevitable. Data center construction will generate concerns over: • Noise • Environmental Impact • Visual Appeal • Loss of land for other purposes • Traffic • Impact on price of local electricity supply 3.4.2 Real Estate Cost Important factors for data center siting include the cost of rent or purchase, utilities, taxes and other operating expenses because they substantially affect the cost of providing cloud services [1].
